extracted.intended_audience: scholars and natural philosophers (mathematicians, anatomists, physicians, natural historians, geologists)
extracted.subtask_description: Reading and assessing multidisciplinary 17th-century scientific reports (mathematical methods, anatomical dissections, medical case reports, natural history, and experimental accounts) for rigor, method, and clarity. Focus on whether procedures, measurements, and interpretations meet the period's standards for reproducibility and explanatory power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Initial approximation closeness and expected correct figures
rubrics_metrics.description: When a is distant from the true root not above a 10th part, then the first figure is rightly assumed; if within a 100th part, the first two figures are right; if within a 1000th part, the first three figures are right.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treated according to the rule, the true figures soon become nine. Use this rule to judge adequacy of the first assumed a and to predict how many correct digits will follow from a given closeness of assumption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and choice of correction formulas (irrational vs rational)
rubrics_metrics.description: The irrational formula (derived from forming the equation from a ± e = z) allows repeated correction and can be further corrected; the rational formula (s b / (ss - tb) ... presented as e = ...) triples the given number of true figures but 'cannot be corrected like the irrational one.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer the irrational form when many further corrected figures are desired because it admits corrective operations; use the rational formula when one multiplication and two divisions (more efficient arithmetically) and rapid tripling of true figures suffice. If more figures are wanted using the rational formula, make a new assumption and repeat the calculation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Efficiency of algebraic operations for corrections
rubrics_metrics.description: Writing the theorem as e = ... is convenient because the business is performed by one multiplication and two divisions, which otherwise would require three multiplications and one division.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select the algebraic formulation that minimizes arithmetic operations for practical computation; note this trade-off when recommending methods for hand calculation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of successive corrections on number of true figures
rubrics_metrics.description: Repeating the calculus always triples the true figures in the assumed a; the first correction quintuples the true figures; the other correction after the first doubles the true figures; on the whole the assumed true figures become seven-fold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these multiplicative expectations to plan how many iterations or which corrections to perform to reach a desired number of accurate figures. The first correction is commonly sufficient for most arithmetical uses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determining sign of correction (e) from equation formation
rubrics_metrics.description: Form an equation from a ± e = z; it will soon appear whether the assumed a be greater or less than just, since se ought always to have a sign contrary to that of the difference between the resolvend and its homogeneum produced from a.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the sign of se relative to the difference between the resolvend and its homogeneum to determine whether the correction e is affirmative or negative. This guides whether to add or subtract the correction to the assumed root.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical recommendation: prefer first correction or new assumption for more digits
rubrics_metrics.description: The rational formula cannot be corrected like the irrational one; so that if more figures of the root be desired, it is better to repeat the calculation by making a new assumption; and then the new quotient, by tripling the number of true figures, will abundantly satisfy even the most scrupulous calculator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When seeking high precision, prefer repeating the calculation with a refined assumption rather than trying to 'correct' the rational formula algebraically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anatomical dissection technique: inflating cavities for observation
rubrics_metrics.description: Having opened the thorax and abdomen by blowing into the aspera arteria, a large cavity or bladder was raised up all along the abdomen ... and fastened to the gizzard, containing in it all the guts and gizzard, but excluding the heart and liver.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use inflation (blowing into the artery) to raise cavities and expose internal arrangements for observation and description. Record method used so others can reproduce the preparation and observations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anatomical illustration standard: life-size figures and detailed labels
rubrics_metrics.description: The proportions of all these parts to each other will be best seen by the following figures, in pl. 14, which are purposely drawn as large as the life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide large, life-size drawings with lettered labels (a, b, c, ...) and captions identifying structures and their relationships. Multiple figures showing different views and magnified details (larynx, bills, glands, etc.) improve clarity and reproducibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Linking anatomy to function by comparative observation
rubrics_metrics.description: The aspera arteria differs from that of most other animals, having not only a larynx at the top, as is usual, but another also at its entrance into the breast, where it is divided, and branches itself into two. From this structure ... it may be that they can so readily imitate human voices; ... their manner of chewing ... shows they ruminate as some quadrupeds do.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reporting anatomical features, compare with other species and propose functional explanations (e.g., special laryngeal structures explain vocal imitation). Such comparative inferences should be grounded in observed structure and behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Case-reporting standard for clinical observations
rubrics_metrics.description: Detailed timeline and prior treatments: e.g., 'After having for about 9 months used many medicines ... in Sept. 1690, applied to me, when I administered some medicines ... In May, 1691 ... began ... to be deprived of her sight ... until August, 1692 ... In July, 1693, she was seized with a fever, when her sight again returned ... Oct. 1693, she has her nocturnal blindness, and her jaundice likewise continues.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide chronological detail, prior remedies tried, sequence of symptoms, associations (e.g., menstrual flux correlated with sight changes), and outcomes. This supports causal inference and reproducibility of clinical observation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clinical/prognostic features and staging of viper envenomation
rubrics_metrics.description: The venom ... though very unhappy and mischievous accidents attend it, as a great tumor, tension and weight of the part, humidity and variety of colours, frenzies, convulsions and vomitings; yet in 8 or 10 days at most these symptoms are over ... In the extreme nervous parts near the pulse and tongue, the bites are dangerous, and the symptoms very painful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report characteristic progression (early syncope, tremblings, convulsions, tingling of ears, transient deafness, mist before eyes), local swelling progression (pea → bean → nut → large tumour → scrotal involvement), timing (3 days to height and ~3 days to abate), and location-based risk to guide prognosis and treatment urgency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Therapeutic protocols for viper bite and other poisons
rubrics_metrics.description: Remedies recommended: drink the decoction of marrubium, fomentation with the decoction applying the rest on the place; Aristolochia is a strong and powerful antidote against the viper, heat a slice and apply to tongue-bite; Pontaeus's antidote (juniper berries extract with decoction of aristolochia roots, succisa, marrubium album, flower of brimstone, and white vitriol) and other prescriptions (use or omit vitriol depending on whether poison is corrosive).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give specific remedial recipes, routes of application (topical, internal), doses where supplied, and note when to add or withhold adjuncts (e.g., vitriol) depending on poison type. Record empirical outcomes (e.g., dog experiments) but with caution about their interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental design standard for evaporation measurements
rubrics_metrics.description: Experiment of quantity of vapour arising simply from the warmth of the water, without being exposed either to sun or wind ... from a surface ... of 8 square inches evaporated during the year 16292 grains of water ... showing depth of water evaporated in one year amounts to 8 inches. Comparison with rainfall measurements at Paris and Lancashire shows sun and wind are much more the causes of evaporation than any internal heat.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Control for external factors (exclude sun and wind), measure a known small surface area over a long continuous interval (a year), aggregate results, and compare with independent rainfall/evaporation observations to infer cause. Note anomalous properties (e.g., vapours adhering to their source surface).

rubrics_metrics.name: Field-reporting standards for geological/geomorphological features
rubrics_metrics.description: Give precise location relative to towns and landmarks; supply dimensions (length ~600 feet at low water, breadth 240–120 feet, heights 15–36 feet); describe composition (many thousand pillars mostly perpendicular), shapes (pentagonal, hexagonal, some 7-sided), diameters (15–24 inches, 2 feet), jointing (columns composed of several joints), surface texture (smooth when washed, rough when not), and arrangement (tops sometimes make even plane surfaces).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide quantitative measurements, note variability and irregularities, describe polygonality and joint morphology, and record surface condition (washed vs unwashed). These details enable comparisons and hypotheses about formation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative morphological criteria for lithic identification
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare the observed pillars with known fossil/stone types: entrochos (columnwise but cylindrical and pith-run), astroites (columnwise, angular, sulcated, pentagonal), and lapis basaltes (similar in formation, substance, size, and standing). Note where they agree and differ (size, presence of pith, sulcation, polygonality, joints).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use multiple morphological axes (shape, jointing, pith, surface sulcation, polygonal count, size/magnitude) to classify and distinguish lithic specimens; explicitly list how the local specimen differs from each comparator to justify taxonomic or genetic inferences.
